hints: Read the wording very carefully. It says between two single water molecules, not how many bonds one water molecule can make with lots of neighbours around it.

Remember what one hydrogen bond needs: a slightly positive H (already bonded to O) on one molecule attracted to a lone pair on the O of the other molecule. Picture how two molecules can line up for this.
walkthrough:
**Recall the structure of one water molecule**

Think of water as bent in shape with one oxygen in the middle. It has two O-H bonds and two lone pairs on the oxygen.

That means one water can donate 2 H-bonds (using its 2 H atoms) and accept 2 H-bonds (using its 2 lone pairs), so up to 4 in total with surrounding molecules.

**Recall what a single hydrogen bond is**

A hydrogen bond forms when the $\delta+$ hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair ($\delta-$ oxygen) of another molecule.

It is one bridge: H (molecule 1) to O lone pair (molecule 2), or the other way round.

**Apply this to just two molecules together**

When you bring only two water molecules together, once one such bridge has formed, those two molecules are already linked and held in position.

They cannot twist to make a second, third or fourth bridge between that same pair without breaking the first one. To use its other H atoms and lone pairs, a water molecule needs a third, fourth and fifth neighbour. So the maximum between that one pair is 1.

options.A: Correct. Only one H-bond bridge can exist at a time directly between any two specific water molecules.
options.B: Not correct. Two is tempting if you count donors and acceptors, but a second bond cannot form between the same two molecules at the same time.
options.C: Not correct. Three or more bonds would need more H atoms and lone pairs lined up between the same pair, which water does not have in the right geometry.
options.D: Not correct. Four is the maximum one water molecule can form with up to four different neighbours in ice, not with one single partner.
